family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start at the node: Oleaceae is woody and usually has opposite or subopposite leaves/branching with no stipules. Then read the leaf architecture and fruit. Local Fraxinus has odd-pinnate compound leaves plus a samara; local Forestiera has simple leaves plus a one-seeded drupe.
core_characters: Trees or shrubs in the local flora.
Leaves usually opposite or subopposite and exstipulate; they may be simple or odd-pinnately compound.
Flowers are usually radial and often small. A 4-merous corolla is common in the family, but the local Fraxinus and Forestiera lineages can be apetalous, so petals are not required.

Oleaceae commonly has 2 stamens, but do not use exact stamen count alone: Forestiera can depart from the simple two-stamen rule, and the Williamson County Forestiera pubescens treatment reports 4–6 stamens in staminate flowers.
Ovary is superior, syncarpous and typically 2-carpellate/2-loculed.
Fruit is highly useful locally: Fraxinus = winged samara; Forestiera = fleshy one-seeded drupe.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach Oleaceae as 'opposite leaves + four white petals.' The two local focal genera often lack a corolla.
Do not teach 'exactly two stamens' as an absolute family rule. It is a strong family tendency, not a safe local absolute.
Do not identify Oleaceae from opposite leaves alone; Rubiaceae, Verbenaceae, Lamiaceae, Bignoniaceae and other families can also be opposite-leaved.
Do not use fruit type as a single family-wide character because Oleaceae includes samaras, drupes, berries and capsules.

Rubiaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves and small flowers can overlap.
Rubiaceae.tie_breaker: Rubiaceae usually has interpetiolar stipules and an inferior ovary; Oleaceae lacks stipules and has a superior ovary.

Bignoniaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves are common and some taxa can be woody.
Bignoniaceae.tie_breaker: Bignoniaceae usually has large bilaterally symmetric tubular flowers and a long capsule with flat winged seeds; local Oleaceae has tiny flowers and either ash samaras or Forestiera drupes.

Lamiaceae / Verbenaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves and small clustered flowers.
Lamiaceae / Verbenaceae.tie_breaker: Check woody habit, exstipulate nodes, flower symmetry, ovary/fruit architecture and especially samara-versus-drupe in the local Oleaceae genera.

fast_key: Opposite woody plant + odd-pinnate compound leaves → inspect for a single-winged samara → Fraxinus.
Opposite/subopposite woody plant + simple leaves → inspect for small dark fleshy drupes and tiny often apetalous flowers → Forestiera.
If opposite leaves are present but interpetiolar stipules are obvious → reconsider Rubiaceae.
If opposite leaves accompany a large showy bilateral trumpet flower and long capsule → reconsider Bignoniaceae.

cards.look_here_first: Look at the branch architecture: opposite to subopposite simple leaves and opposite branchlets. Then look for very early, apetalous flowers before leaf-out or dark bluish-purple drupes later.
confirm: Leaves simple, usually opposite/subopposite, without stipules.
Flowers functionally unisexual and the plants are dioecious.
Corolla absent; the tiny flowers can appear as exposed stamens or pistils on bare twigs.
Williamson County treatment reports 4–6 stamens in staminate flowers, a useful warning against overlearning the usual Oleaceae two-stamen rule.
Fruit is a fleshy dark drupe with one stone.

cards.look_here_first: Opposite branching and odd-pinnate leaves establish ash; in fruit, look for the smaller samara whose wing is terminal or only slightly decurrent onto the seed body.
confirm: Usually 5–7 leaflets in the Central Texas comparison.
Lower leaflet surface often pale/glaucous and useful in comparison with green ash.
Samara body is relatively small; wing is terminal or only slightly decurrent.
Leaf-scar/bud form is useful when fruit is unavailable.
cards.taxonomy_note: Current POWO accepts Fraxinus albicans; Fraxinus texensis is a synonym. Some reusable image sources remain filed under F. texensis.

cards.look_here_first: Opposite branching and odd-pinnate leaves establish ash; then look for the larger green-ash samara whose wing runs distinctly down the seed body and for denser samara clusters.
confirm: Commonly 5–7(9) leaflets in the Central Texas comparison.
Samara wing is clearly decurrent down the fruit body, unlike Texas ash's mostly terminal wing.
Samaras often occur in denser clusters than Texas ash.
Leaf-scar shape and bud position are important on non-fruiting trees.

cards.look_here_first: A densely branched shrub with opposite elbow-like branchlets and very narrow, leathery, mostly opposite simple leaves; confirm with apetalous early flowers and a black one-seeded drupe.
confirm: Leaves are narrow/linear, entire, leathery and somewhat revolute.
Flowers are tiny, dioecious and lack petals.
Fruit is a small black one-seeded drupe.

strongest_visual_sequence: 1. Node/branch architecture: opposite or subopposite, no stipules.
2. Fraxinus leaf: odd-pinnate compound leaf with rachis and leaflets.
3. Fraxinus fruit: single-winged samara; compare Texas ash vs green ash wing decurrence.
5. Forestiera flower: tiny, early and apetalous on bare twigs.
7. Look-alike card: Oleaceae exstipulate node vs Rubiaceae interpetiolar stipule.
